title: The self to be trained
hookLine: the self that commands evil, that blames itself, that is at peace (12:53; 75:2; 89:27)

cards: It's eleven at night. One voice in you says: one more episode, one more slice, send the angry text, you deserve it. Ten minutes later, another: why did you do that?
You always do that. And once in a while, on a good day, there's a third thing, not really a voice at all. A quiet.
You did the right thing, or you didn't and you've made it right, and you're simply at rest. Everyone knows those three.
The Qur'an names them, in three different surahs, and Sufis built a whole map of the inner life on them.

teach.b: The Arabic word is nafs: soul, self, or ego, depending on the sentence. The first nafs is in the story of Yusuf. In Pickthall's translation: "the (human) soul enjoineth unto evil," except where God has mercy.

Commentators differ on who says those words, Yusuf or the wife of the man who bought him, but all agree on what they describe: the self that pushes, that grabs, that wants now. An-nafs al-ammarah, the self that commands.
The second is in a short Meccan surah, where God swears an oath by it: "Nay, I swear by the accusing soul."
An-nafs al-lawwamah, the self that blames: the voice at eleven-ten. God swears by it. The conscience that stings is honored, not despised.
The third comes near the end of surah 89, addressed with great tenderness: "But ah! thou soul at peace!" An-nafs al-mutma'innah, the self at rest, invited to return to its Lord, content.
Sufi teachers read the three as stages. The self isn't evil, and it isn't thrown away. It's trained, the way you'd train a strong young horse: not broken, but taught.

The work of the path is moving from commanding, through blaming, toward peace. A hadith in al-Bukhari fits: the strong one isn't the one who wins the wrestling match, but the one who controls himself when angry.

how: Muslims speak of struggling with the nafs as a lifelong part of faith, and Sufi teachers guide students through its stages, commanding, blaming and at peace, with remembrance, self-examination and service.

o: the breath of life God blew into Adam
an evil spirit that whispers people into sin
the self: commanding, blaming, or at peace

games.q: the three selves — tap the pairs.

s: Sufis teach that the self should be thrown away
it's trained, like a strong young horse: not broken, but taught.
in the Qur'an, God swears by the blaming self
nay, I swear by the accusing soul.
commentators all agree Yusuf says the line about the soul enjoining evil
they differ: Yusuf, or the wife of the man who bought him.

games.q: your blaming self is stinging you for something you did yesterday. what does the Qur'an do with that voice?
games.why: nay, I swear by the accusing soul (75:2). the conscience that stings is honored, a stage on the way to peace.

practice: Replay your day so far and name each self that spoke: the commanding one, pushing for more, faster, now; the blaming one, stinging, maybe too harshly; and any moment of quiet, even a few seconds.
Name them without judging them, and thank the blaming self for caring. If you pray, you can ask God to bring your self to peace.

wordCard.voice: Nafs. The self, in three stages in the Qur'an: commanding, blaming, and at peace. Today's word.
